difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → cost reduction → increased adoption). The correct weakener attacks the move from cost reduction to adoption, leaving the cost-reduction premise intact. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope economic fact, and a narrowly scoped premise attack.
stimulus: A government economist argued that the new tax credit for residential solar panel installation will substantially increase the proportion of households that use solar energy. She reasoned that the credit will reduce the upfront cost of installation by nearly 30 percent, and that high upfront cost has historically been the primary barrier preventing homeowners from adopting solar technology.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of homeowners who declined to install solar panels found that a majority cited concerns about long-term maintenance costs rather than upfront installation costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tax credit applies only to installations completed by licensed contractors, and licensed contractors are available in most regions of the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries that have offered similar upfront subsidies for solar installation have seen dramatic increases in residential solar adoption within three years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The federal government has introduced tax credits for energy-efficient appliances in the same fiscal year as the solar credit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Solar panel technology has improved significantly over the past decade, making panels more efficient than those available when the cost barrier was first identified.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument depends on the premise that high upfront cost is the primary barrier to adoption. Answer A directly undercuts this by showing that most homeowners who declined to install solar panels cited ongoing maintenance costs—not upfront cost—as their obstacle. If the credit doesn't address the actual primary barrier, it is unlikely to drive the predicted increase in adoption.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it attacks the load-bearing premise that upfront cost is the primary barrier, showing that maintenance costs dominate homeowner objections. Removing the upfront cost obstacle won't eliminate the actual deterrent.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. That licensed contractors are widely available is, if anything, a mild strengthener (it rules out an access barrier), not a weakener.
explanations.C: Opposite answer / strengthener. International precedent supporting upfront subsidies bolsters the economist's prediction rather than undermining it.
explanations.D: Irrelevant / shift in subject. The existence of concurrent appliance credits doesn't bear on whether the solar credit will increase solar adoption; this is an accurate but unconnected fact.
explanations.E: Too narrow / wrong direction. Improved efficiency could, if anything, make solar more attractive—a mild strengthener—and it does not address the premise-to-conclusion move about cost barriers.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on historical correlation in a medical context. The correct weakener introduces a disanalogy between the historical sample and the target population, attacking the move from evidence to conclusion without touching either empirical premise in isolation. Distractors include a strengthener and a plausible but tangential medical fact.
stimulus: Researchers at a large urban hospital observed that patients who were assigned a dedicated case manager during the first week of hospitalization had significantly shorter average stays than patients who received standard care. The hospital's administrators concluded that assigning case managers to all newly admitted patients would reduce the hospital's average length of stay system-wide.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the administrators' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Case managers at the hospital are currently assigned only to patients whose conditions are judged, at admission, to be the least medically complex.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that have universally implemented case management programs have reported reductions in average length of stay comparable to those observed at the urban hospital.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of hiring sufficient case managers to cover all newly admitted patients would exceed the savings generated by shorter hospital stays during the first year of implementation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the case managers at the hospital have advanced clinical training in addition to their administrative credentials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who receive standard care at the hospital are still assigned a primary nurse responsible for coordinating their discharge planning.

explanations.correct: The administrators assume the observed benefit of case management can be generalized to all patients. Answer A reveals a critical disanalogy: the case managers were assigned only to the least complex patients—precisely those most likely to have short stays regardless. The correlation between case management and shorter stays may therefore reflect patient selection, not the case managers' effect. Expanding case management to all patients, including complex ones, would not be expected to produce the same result.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it exposes a selection-bias confound. The positive outcome was observed in a skewed sample (low-complexity patients), so the administrators cannot validly generalize the effect to the full patient population.
explanations.B: Opposite answer / strengthener. External evidence that universal case management works elsewhere directly supports the administrators' conclusion.
explanations.C: Shift in subject / irrelevant. Cost-effectiveness is a separate consideration from whether the policy would reduce length of stay; the conclusion is about clinical outcomes, not financial returns.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. The credentials of individual case managers don't bear on whether the effect observed in the study will generalize to all new admissions.
explanations.E: Too narrow. The existence of discharge-planning nurses describes standard care but does not address the selection-bias problem or otherwise undermine the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Analogical argument in an environmental-science context predicting that a successful invasive-species intervention in one region will succeed in another. The correct weakener attacks the analogy by identifying a relevant disanalogy. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope ecological fact, and a narrowly scoped distractor that attacks a peripheral premise.
stimulus: Wildlife officials in the Pacific Northwest introduced a targeted biological control agent—a host-specific parasitic wasp—to suppress populations of the invasive emerald ash borer beetle in forested areas of Oregon. Within four years, ash borer populations in treated areas declined by over 70 percent, and native ash tree survival rates improved markedly. Based on this success, conservation groups have urged officials to deploy the same wasp in the forests of the upper Midwest, where the ash borer has devastated native ash populations.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument for deploying the parasitic wasp in the upper Midwest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The parasitic wasp requires overwintering temperatures above a threshold that is regularly exceeded in Oregon but that upper Midwest forests frequently fall below, preventing the wasp from establishing a self-sustaining population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The emerald ash borer has caused greater cumulative damage to native ash populations in the upper Midwest than in Oregon, suggesting that intervention is more urgently needed in the Midwest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biological control programs using host-specific parasites have, in general, a strong record of avoiding harm to non-target insect species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oregon wildlife officials consulted with entomologists at three universities before approving the wasp introduction program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native ash trees in the upper Midwest belong to the same genus as those in Oregon, though they include several distinct regional species.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: because the wasp worked in Oregon, it will work in the Midwest. Answer A identifies a decisive disanalogy—climatic incompatibility. The wasp cannot survive Midwest winters, so it cannot establish a self-sustaining population there. This directly undermines the core premise that the Oregon intervention is a reliable model for the Midwest deployment.
explanations.A: Correct. This is the weakener: it attacks the analogy by revealing that the key mechanism (a persistent wasp population suppressing the beetle) cannot replicate in the Midwest due to climatic differences, making the Oregon success non-transferable.
explanations.B: Opposite answer / strengthener. Greater urgency of the problem in the Midwest, if anything, supports the case for deploying the wasp there, bolstering rather than undermining the argument.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The general safety record of host-specific biological controls neither supports nor undermines the conclusion about whether this particular wasp will be effective in the Midwest. It addresses a different concern (non-target harm), not the effectiveness question.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The procedural care taken in Oregon speaks to the quality of the Oregon program's design but has no bearing on whether conditions in the Midwest are suitable for replication.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Taxonomic similarity of the host trees is a minor point about the target ecosystem; it does not address whether the wasp can survive Midwest winters or effectively suppress the beetle there.
